source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Pretrained models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false when the format is right. Calibration rises with model size and with few-shot examples. Zero-shot is worse.
numbers: Models 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B. BIG-Bench and MMLU 5-shot. Calibration poor 0-shot, better few-shot.
limits: Pretrained base models only. Not the RLHF chat models people use now.
agent_relevance: Confidence is usable only after the question is put in a calibrated format. Fix the format in code.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Replacing one answer option with 'none of the above' cut accuracy a lot and harmed calibration, even for the 52B model, even 20-shot.
numbers: 52B, MMLU: accuracy drop shown in Fig 36; 5-shot and 20-shot both failed to fix it.
quote: models seem to be confused by a "none of the above" option
limits: A dissociation between knowing and reporting. Exact drop size is in a figure, not in text.
agent_relevance: Never ask the agent to say 'none of these'. Use a separate code-checked abstain step.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Helpful-harmless RLHF policies look badly miscalibrated, but one temperature (T=2.5) fixes calibration on several tasks.
numbers: Same T=2.5 for all evaluations (MMLU, MMLU true/false, TruthfulQA).
limits: Only one RLHF recipe, early 2022. Stronger RL may distort more.
agent_relevance: Miscalibration of chat models may be a scale problem, fixable by simple post-hoc rescaling done in code.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(True): the model proposes an answer, then rates its own answer true or false. It separates right from wrong samples. Showing it 5 of its own T=1 samples first (brainstorm other options) helps clearly. Calibration is poor zero-shot and good 20-shot.
numbers: 52B, five sampling tasks (TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, Codex HumanEval), equal weight. Filtering to P(True)>0.5 raised accuracy on each task (Fig 1).
quote: 'brainstorming other possibilities' helps large models to evaluate the validity of a given answer option
limits: Exact AUROC values are in figures. Model cannot tell its own tokens from given tokens (authors' footnote).
agent_relevance: Supports G4 caution (own samples) but shows that a consider-alternatives view before rating helps. Mirrors 'consider the opposite' in humans.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK): a value head trained to predict whether the model will answer a question correctly. It works in distribution, partly transfers to new tasks, but calibration breaks out of distribution. It rises when source text or hints are in context. Asking in words ('how confident could you answer?') gave no big gain out of distribution in early tests.
numbers: Trained on 30 samples at T=1 per TriviaQA question (soft label from count correct), 10-shot prompt. 52B model. Evaluated OOD on Arithmetic, Python synthesis, Lambada.
limits: Authors flag that the head may learn 'how hard is this question' rather than 'do I know it'. Needs weights access.
agent_relevance: A trained 'do I know' probe is the machine version of feeling-of-knowing, and like human FOK it works from question features. For an API agent it is not available; use sample agreement.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, a verbalized probability is better calibrated than the sample-based probability. Sampled 'label probability' is overconfident.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo SciQ ECE: label prob 0.256, verbalized 1-stage top-4 0.065. TruthfulQA ECE: label 0.451, verbalized top-4 0.203. TriviaQA ECE 0.140 vs 0.050 (top-2). Label prob used n=10 samples.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Calibration (ECE) only. On TruthfulQA label-prob AUC was 0.418, below chance; verbalized AUC 0.455-0.545 also near chance. ECE can look good with useless confidence.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence is cheap and better calibrated than raw sample frequency, but TruthfulQA shows neither tracks truth when the model holds a common misconception.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: Asking for the top-k guesses with a probability for each (consider alternatives, as in human 'consider the opposite') cuts ECE further, mostly on harder data. Two-stage and CoT variants were not better.
numbers: gpt-3.5 SciQ ECE: top-1 0.234, top-2 0.132, top-4 0.065. TruthfulQA ECE-t top-1 0.256, top-2 0.115. gpt-4 TriviaQA: label ECE 0.078 AUC 0.950; verbalized top-1 ECE 0.024 AUC 0.937. Verb 2S CoT on gpt-3.5 TriviaQA ECE 0.110, worse than 1S top-2 0.050.
limits: Gains on AUC are small or none; the gain is calibration, not resolution. Only QA tasks.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt: list several answers with probabilities. Helps calibration. Do not count it as better error detection.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: Linguistic confidence words ('likely') mapped to probabilities with held-out data can be very well calibrated, but the human-survey mapping can be bad.
numbers: gpt-3.5 SciQ ECE: 'optimised' mapping 0.064, human-survey mapping 0.166. Llama2-70B-chat TruthfulQA ECE: optimised 0.047 vs human mapping 0.376. Human mapping from 123 survey respondents.
limits: Needs a calibration set to learn the mapping. AUC about the same as numeric.
agent_relevance: If the agent uses words, map them to numbers with measured accuracy, not human intuition.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Verbalized confidence is overconfident and clusters at 80-100%, mostly in multiples of 5, like human talk. Failure prediction is near chance for plain verbalized confidence.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA 2), 8 datasets. GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 average AUROC only 62.7%. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
limits: Older models; results vary by dataset. GPT-4 ECE is low on trivia (see c07).
agent_relevance: Do not use a single verbalized score as an error detector. Treat as a weak prior.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
finding: CoT and other human-inspired prompts lower ECE, but mostly because accuracy rose while confidence stayed at 80-100%. Failure prediction stayed close to AUROC 0.5. Lower ECE here does not mean better resolution.
numbers: GPT-4 on GSM8K with CoT: 93.6% accuracy, ECE 0.064 by giving 100% to every sample, so no discrimination.
limits: Shows ECE can be gamed by constant confidence. Prompt effect shrinks as the model grows.
agent_relevance: Judge any confidence signal by AUROC (resolution), not ECE alone. This is the calibration vs resolution split from human work.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Sampling several answers and measuring agreement gives much better failure prediction than one verbalized score, especially on arithmetic. Gains flatten after about 5 to 13 samples.
numbers: GPT-3.5, CoT + consistency, M=5. GSM8K AUROC 54.8% (single verbalized) to 92.7%. Average over 5 datasets AUROC 56.4% (Top-K, M=1) to 73.0% (Prompt M=5) or 69.6% (Self-Random M=5). M from 1 to 13 tested.
limits: Professional law and other knowledge-heavy tasks stayed hard. No single method won everywhere. White-box gap narrow: AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605.
agent_relevance: Agreement across samples is the best black-box signal for reasoning tasks. Fits G4: still only a hint, since samples are correlated.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Mixing verbalized confidence into the consistency vote helps when sampling is limited. Best aggregation depends on the metric: Pair-Rank gives low ECE (down to 0.028), Avg-Conf gives best failure prediction.
numbers: M=5 queries. Lowest ECE reported 0.028. Gap to white-box methods narrow.
limits: Needs 5x cost. Different aggregators win ECE vs AUROC.
agent_relevance: Pick the aggregator for the job: selection needs resolution, reporting needs calibration.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Reasoning models are better calibrated than their non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings (6 model pairs, 6 datasets), and calibration improves as the chain of thought goes on.
numbers: TriviaQA ECE: Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.129 vs R1-Distill-Qwen 0.042; Qwen3 non-thinking 0.207 vs thinking 0.063. NonambigQA ECE: Qwen3 0.403 vs 0.226. 1,000 examples per dataset.
quote: strictly better confidence calibration than their non-reasoning counterparts in 33 out of the 36 settings
limits: Ablations at ~32B only; greedy decoding in main runs. Reasoning models rarely state confidence below 55%. Multiple-choice datasets let non-reasoning models win AUROC in a few cases.
agent_relevance: Slow thinking with alternatives and backtracking makes the confidence signal better. Supports a doubt-on-signal design (G1) over fixed rechecks.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Ablation on R1-Distill-Qwen-32B: removing non-linear reasoning (trying alternatives, backtracking) hurts calibration most. Teaching slow thinking in context to non-reasoning models also improves calibration.
numbers: TriviaQA ECE: original 0.042; minus non-linear reasoning 0.161; no CoT 0.150. NonambigQA ECE 0.195 vs 0.341 vs 0.359. In-context slow thinking: GLM-4-32B TriviaQA ECE 0.150 to 0.029, AUROC 0.631 to 0.796; Qwen2.5-32B ECE 0.135 to 0.091.
limits: Removing epistemic markers raised ECE but raised AUROC (0.782 to 0.837), so the two metrics disagree. One model ablated. Forcing longer CoT (budget forcing) did not reliably help.
agent_relevance: A prompt that makes the agent try an alternative before rating confidence can be added cheaply. Test it at equal tokens (G7).

source: Hiremath & Hiremath (2026) Calibration Drift Under Reasoning
finding: Claims the opposite of c13: past some chain-of-thought budget, models become overconfident because long chains lock into a wrong hypothesis. The data are weak: for Llama-3.1-8B ECE falls with budget, not a U shape.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B ECE 0.104 (light), 0.050 (medium), 0.015 (heavy); accuracy 0.732 light vs 0.653 medium. 47 questions, three seeds. Llama-3.3-70B only no-reasoning.
limits: Tiny sample (47 questions), authors call it illustrative. Preprint, weak evidence. Conflicts with c13.
agent_relevance: The conflict is unsettled. Keep a code-side check (G3) rather than trusting rising confidence in long chains.

source: Prasad & Nguyen (2025) When Two LLMs Debate, Both Think They'll Win
finding: In zero-sum debates, models start overconfident and raise confidence as arguments are exchanged, instead of lowering it. Mutual 75%+ win claims happen in most debates.
numbers: 60 three-round debates, 10 LLMs. Initial mean confidence 72.9% vs rational 50%. Final round about 83%. Both sides claimed 75% or more in 61.7% of debates. Self-debate (identical copies): 64.1% to 75.2%. Told chance is exactly 50%: 50.0% to 57.1%.
limits: One task type (policy debate); self-reported 0-100 bets. Private scratchpad sometimes disagreed with public rating.
agent_relevance: Confidence rises with commitment and argument volume, not with evidence. Never let the agent's confidence rise over rounds without a new passing check (G2, G3).

source: Michael, BenShushan, Bien & Moore (2026) Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
finding: Preregistered study finds LLMs are overconfident on average and show a hard-easy effect like humans: overconfidence grows with difficulty, easy items show underconfidence. Explained as confidence responding less to difficulty than accuracy does.
numbers: 11 models. Across all question sets: stated confidence 88%, accuracy 79%, so 9 points overconfident. LifeEval at smallest radius (hardest): confidence 34.2% vs actual 9.6%. At 20-year radius: confidence 80.5% vs actual 92.0%.
limits: LifeEval ceiling is 56.8% (a Bayesian task about age at death), so generalising is limited. Preprint. Authors cite regression to the mean as the most parsimonious human explanation.
agent_relevance: Confidence needs per-difficulty re-scaling. A single global threshold will over-trust on hard items and over-doubt easy ones.

source: Michael, BenShushan, Bien & Moore (2026) Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
finding: Reasoning models track accuracy much more closely than chat models, though a hard-easy slope remains.
numbers: LifeEval: reasoning models ECE 0.025 to 0.063 (mean 0.037), score 54.2%, mean confidence 53.5%. Chat Claude Haiku 3 ECE 0.267, confidence 79.8%. Correlation of stated confidence with actual probability: 0.94 for 5 reasoning models, 0.48 for others. Multiples of 5: 91.4% for chat vs 61.1% for reasoning. Hard-easy slope mean 0.168 (Claude Sonnet 4 0.327, DeepSeek-R1 0.053).
limits: Different task from c13 but same direction.
agent_relevance: Supports c13 across labs. The hard-easy slope still needs a correction in code.

source: Ghosh & Panday (2026) The Dunning-Kruger Effect in Large Language Models
finding: Weak models are far more overconfident than strong ones: confidence stays near ceiling whatever the accuracy.
numbers: 4 models, 4 benchmarks, 1,500 questions per model per dataset (24,000 trials). Kimi K2 accuracy 23.3%, mean confidence 95.7%, ECE 0.726. Claude Haiku 4.5 accuracy 75.4%, ECE 0.122. Gemini 2.5 Pro accuracy 80.9%, confidence 99.5%, ECE 0.185.
limits: Preprint, one prompt format. 'Dunning-Kruger' is an analogy; here it is plain ceiling-level confidence. Low accuracy may partly reflect output-format failures (not checked).
agent_relevance: A weak sub-model in a cascade will not warn you. Never route on the weak model's own confidence alone.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know (Nature Machine Intelligence)
finding: People overrate LLM answers when shown default explanations. Longer explanations raise confidence without raising accuracy. Rewriting explanations to match model confidence shrinks both the calibration and discrimination gaps. This is a fluency cue acting on the human monitor of the machine.
numbers: Human-confidence ECE with default explanations: .264 GPT-3.5, .291 PaLM2, .165 GPT-4o; model's own .104, .154, .141. Modified explanations: .150, .225, .111. Human AUC .589-.602 default, .652-.694 modified; model AUC .746-.781. N=41, 39, 42 (default), 60, 60, 59 (modified). Long vs short explanation BF=25.
limits: Human accuracy on the questions did not improve. Humans knew about as much as models (51% vs 52% on GPT-3.5 items).
agent_relevance: Output style is a cue the reader uses (fluency illusion). The agent's report to a human should carry calibrated hedges, not extra length.

source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and LLMs
finding: Review: LLM implicit confidence (token likelihood, consistency) tracks trial-by-trial accuracy better than verbal confidence; fine-tuned sensitivity is domain-specific. Human sensitivity does not improve with feedback while bias does.
numbers: GPT-3.5 token-likelihood AUC 0.778 (MMLU); GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned verbal AUC 0.83 (TriviaQA); both called modest. Cash et al. 2025 found similar LLM and human sensitivity but with a metric confounded by accuracy.
limits: A review, no new experiments. Fluency and feeling-of-knowing are not covered directly.
agent_relevance: Gap between what is represented and what is stated. Read implicit signals in code where possible.

source: Steyvers, Belem & Smyth (2025) Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models
finding: Fine-tuning on self-consistency targets (not ground truth) improves verbal confidence AUC and ECE in domain and partly out of domain. Training single-question confidence did not transfer to pairwise comparison, and the reverse.
numbers: GPT-4.1-mini MMLU-PRO AUC 0.52 to 0.68, ECE 0.61 to 0.05; GSM8K AUC 0.53 to 0.76, ECE 0.75 to 0.04; TriviaQA AUC 0.75 to 0.83. Out of domain TruthfulQA ECE worsened 0.10 to 0.18. Cross-task transfer: TruthfulQA AUC 0.67 to 0.63. Multitask raised OOD AUC 0.73 to 0.76 (p<0.05). Llama3.1-70B OOD AUC 0.70 to 0.74.
limits: Only two models; training target is sampling agreement. Metacognitive skills look task-specific, not one faculty.
agent_relevance: Single-question confidence and comparing two answers are two different skills. Use the right one for each slot.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration for open models. Fine-tuning with LoRA on a small graded set gives much better ECE and AUROC; about 1000 graded examples already beat baselines.
numbers: Open-ended MMLU; LLaMA-2 7B/13B, Mistral 7B, LLaMA-3. Training set sampled to about 20,000, 2,000 held out for temperature; gains slow after about 5,000. Sampling methods: good ECE, weak AUROC. Verbal elicitation: decent AUROC, poor ECE even after temperature scaling.
limits: Needs weights. Prompting methods' ECE did not improve as the base model improved; AUROC improved slightly.
agent_relevance: Calibration and resolution come from different methods, as in humans. We cannot fine-tune, so choose by purpose.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Uncertainty is not strictly self-knowledge. Mistral 7B predicted LLaMA-2 7B's correctness better than LLaMA-2 7B did itself, and sentence embeddings were competitive with the model's own features. In a user study, people used the confidence scores when they were reliable.
numbers: Mistral applied to LLaMA-2 7B has higher AUROC than LLaMA-2 on itself. User study N=181 participants, 20 per variant (as stated in the paper).
limits: Preliminary user study. Crowd workers.
agent_relevance: A second model can judge the agent's answer about as well as the agent can, which matches the no-self-grading rule (G2, G5).

source: Liu et al. (2025) MetaFaith: Faithful Natural Language Uncertainty Expression in LLMs (EMNLP 2025)
finding: Models sound assertive when they are wrong: the words do not match their internal confidence. Standard prompting helps a little, factuality-based calibration can hurt, and a prompt method inspired by human metacognition helps most.
numbers: Up to 61% improvement in faithfulness; 83% win rate over original generations, judged by humans (abstract-level numbers only).
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Other numbers not checked.
agent_relevance: Word choice in the agent's report is a separate channel from its numeric score; check them against each other in code.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Relying on the Unreliable: The Impact of Language Models' Reluctance to Express Uncertainty
finding: Models rarely express doubt, and when they use certainty words they are often wrong. The overconfidence comes from RLHF preferences that penalise uncertain wording.
numbers: 9 models, 49 prompts, 284 MMLU questions, 125,244 queries. Answers with strengtheners: 53% correct. Answers with weakeners: 32% correct. 17% of wrong answers had strengtheners. Average 47% error among confident responses. Reward-model scores: plain 4.03, strengtheners 0.82, weakeners -1.86. Users relied on 81% of strengtheners though 66% were right.
limits: MMLU only. The human experiment used scripted conditions. Last 15% of the page not read.
agent_relevance: Do not train or prompt the agent to look confident. Reward models punish doubt, so doubt must be forced by the program.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: When the model is told to review its own answer without external feedback, accuracy goes down, because it flips more right answers to wrong than the reverse. Gains in earlier work came from using the true label to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3.
limits: Prompted review of one answer, with no code check.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G1 and G2: a self-doubt step with no signal is harmful. Self-monitoring without a real check does not help.

source: Li, Xiong, Wu & Hooi (2025) ConfTuner (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Training verbalized confidence with a proper scoring rule (tokenized Brier) calibrates it and the gain carries to downstream control. Confidence below 0.5 triggers a revision, and low-confidence samples get sent to a stronger model.
numbers: Up to 54.7% ECE and 14.4% AUROC improvement over best baseline. Cascade to GPT-4o: up to 9.3% (HotpotQA) and 5.5% (TruthfulQA) higher refined accuracy at the same revision budget (100-400 samples). Self-correction: baselines gave marginal or negative gains because they put low confidence on right answers and so edited right answers.
limits: Needs fine-tuning. Self-correction tested on HotpotQA and TruthfulQA only.
agent_relevance: Confidence-gated revision works only when confidence has resolution. Poor confidence makes revision hurt. Matches Huang (c27).

source: Verbalized Confidence Triggers Self-Verification: Emergent Behavior Without Explicit Reasoning Supervision (2025)
finding: Training only on a scalar confidence label (fraction of 10 samples correct) makes small models verify themselves more when confidence is low, with no reasoning supervision. Calibration and accuracy improve.
numbers: LLaMA3.2-3B GSM8K: AUROC 50.57 to 81.25, ECE 0.2065 to 0.0568; MATH-500 accuracy 41.2 to 56.6, ECE 0.473 to 0.178. Self-verification 20% of outputs vs under 1.5% zero-shot. Training set 0.75k examples, K=10.
limits: Small models; no seeds or variance reported. Qwen2.5-1.5B gains small (MATH-500 +1.4 accuracy points). Some low-confidence outputs loop.
agent_relevance: Confidence as a control signal that triggers checking: the same pattern as our impasse trigger, learned by training.

source: Kim & Kang (2026) Same Answer, Different Confidence: Protocol Sensitivity in LLM Calibration
finding: Whether verbalized or token-likelihood confidence 'wins' depends on measurement protocol. In a twelve-study audit, five never state which context the token score was read in.
numbers: 4 QA datasets, 3 models of 7-8B. Changing the token-score context flips the winner in 4 of 12 settings under ECE and 9 of 12 under AUROC. Using an accepted TriviaQA alias instead of the canonical string changes verbalized confidence by 0.072 although both are correct.
limits: Small open models only. Concerns comparisons, not absolute quality.
agent_relevance: Any calibration number for our agent must fix the answer string, context and label. Otherwise gains may be protocol noise.

source: Garden-path judgment-of-learning preprint, Huff lab, Tuebingen (2025): Judgment of learning in generative AI
finding: Human judgments of learning predicted later recognition. GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o judgments did not.
numbers: Humans N=78 (power analysis about 69). Slope of JOL on recognition in the fitting context: human B=0.167, 95% CI [0.018, 0.316]; GPT-3.5 B=0.013 [-0.147, 0.172]; GPT-4-turbo B=0.026 [-0.143, 0.194]; GPT-4o B=0.045 [-0.159, 0.248]. Models at temperature 1, 100 runs each, zero-shot.
limits: The LLM never memorised anything, so it predicts a task it did not do. One task, one prompt style. Direct test of an old paradigm.
agent_relevance: No evidence that an LLM's 'will I remember this' judgment tracks anything. Do not ask the agent to predict its own future performance.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (ACL Findings 2025)
finding: Weighting the majority vote by the model's own confidence (CISC) reaches the same accuracy with fewer samples. The best confidence for this is P(True), which is not the best calibrated one. Resolution within one question matters, not ECE.
numbers: 9 open models, 4 datasets (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU-Pro, BBH). Cost cut at budget 5 / 10: P(True) 41% / 46%, response probability 22% / 31%, verbal 0-100 22% / 30%, verbal binary 18% / 10%. Within-question discrimination: P(True) 62.3%, verbal 0-100 56.1%, verbal binary 52.2%. Accuracy gain 1.6% (P(True), budget 5). 30 paths per question.
limits: Needs token probabilities for P(True). Accuracy gains are small (0.2-1.6 points). Human check only on 90 responses.
agent_relevance: Confidence used as a vote weight inside a sampling loop. Test it in our selector as a tiebreak (G5), with weights computed in code.

source: BrowseConf (2025): confidence-guided test-time scaling for search agents
finding: In long agent runs, verbalized confidence ranks answers but is overconfident in absolute terms. A rule that retries the question when confidence is below a threshold approaches the accuracy of sampling 10 answers with about half the attempts.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek-V3.1 on BrowseComp, up to 10 attempts. gpt-oss BC: Pass@1 33.8, self-consistency(10) 47.5, CISC(10) 52.2, BrowseConf-Neg 54.5 with 3.87 attempts on average. DeepSeek BC: Pass@1 29.5, CISC 38.7, BrowseConf-Neg 41.8 with 5.72 attempts. Accuracy near zero below 70% confidence; top 90-94% bin only 53.33% accurate. Threshold tuned on 500 SailorFog-QA samples.
limits: Pass@10 is 68.6-70.3%, far above any confidence method. The summary variant becomes overconfident in a wrong first answer. Threshold from a different dataset.
agent_relevance: A working example of a confidence gate inside an agent loop, tuned in code. Low confidence is a good retry trigger even when absolute values are off.

source: Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (2026)
finding: Models do not use their own stated confidence to decide whether to answer or abstain. Raising the penalty for wrong answers barely changes behaviour, and telling them to use the confidence changed nothing. Applying the optimal rule afterwards in code raises utility.
numbers: 10 models on HLE, GPQA Diamond, GSM8K; penalty lambda 0.1 to 100. HLE high penalty (lambda 10 or more): GPT-5-nano utility -0.688 to -0.004 under the optimal rule; GPT-4.1-mini -0.853 to -0.169. Gains up to +0.685. GSM8K gains near 0 (-0.003 to +0.019). Subsets of 128 for HLE and GSM8K.
limits: LLM grader; verbal confidence as a proxy; verifiable tasks only.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G5/G6-style design: the decision to stop or answer is made by code from the signal, not by the model. Monitor and controller are dissociated inside the model.
